Where it began

Lasith Malinga was born on 28 August 1983 and grew up in Rathgama, a coastal village a few miles up the road from Galle, where the whole place seemed to play cricket. He learned the game with friends on the sandbanks and among the coconut palms beside the river, with a tennis ball, and he has said that was where his famous round-arm action came from.

He went to school at Vidyaloka College and then Mahinda College in Galle. At Vidyaloka the former Sri Lanka fast bowler Champaka Ramanayake spotted him and brought him to Galle Cricket Club. An early attempt to make his arm more upright cost him pace and direction, so he went back to the action nature gave him, with Ramanayake's blessing. His club team-mates called him daakaththa, the sickle.

The player

His Test debut, against Australia at Darwin in July 2004, brought six wickets, among them Adam Gilchrist and Shane Warne. Gilchrist came to the Sri Lankan dressing room afterwards to give him one of the stumps. He became Sri Lanka's fastest Test bowler and played 30 Tests between 2004 and 2010, taking 101 wickets at 33.16 with three five-wicket innings and a best of 5 for 50. He gave up Tests in April 2011 so he could keep playing the shorter formats for longer.

What made him special

The sling, the pace and above all the yorker. He could land the ball on a batter's toes again and again, and dip his slower one late. At the 2007 World Cup he took four South African wickets in four balls, Shaun Pollock, Andrew Hall, Jacques Kallis and Makhaya Ntini, and in 2019 he did it again in a T20 international against New Zealand, the only man to manage it twice. He took five international hat-tricks in all, captained Sri Lanka to the T20 World Cup title in 2014, and was the first bowler to reach 100 T20I wickets.

Batting was more of a hobby. He made a single Test fifty, a 64, which was surely mentioned more than once in the dressing room.

Away from the middle

He led the attack for the Mumbai Indians for years, became the first bowler to reach 100 wickets in the IPL, and was later their bowling coach. He also coached the fast bowlers at Rajasthan Royals. In retirement he gave his time to two passions: music, with a debut album, Life, in 2023 and many songs in Sinhala and Hindi since, and koi carp, which he collects and breeds and calls his biggest hobby.

And finally

He set up a YouTube channel in 2020 to talk about cricket, and in time it carried regular news of his fish as well. A man who spent his career aiming at batters' feet seems to have found contentment watching carp glide past his own.
